63569.etyen:
The lowercase form of U. From Latin V, from an Old Italic form of Ancient Greek Υ (U, “upsilon”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤅 (w, “waw; hook”). In medieval Latin-script writing, ⟨u⟩ and ⟨v⟩ were positional forms of a single letter; they later became distinct letters, with ⟨u⟩ used for the vowel. / The uppercase form of u. From Latin V, as a later rounded graphic variant of the same letter, from an Old Italic form of Ancient Greek Υ (U, “upsilon”), ultimately from Phoenician 𐤅 (w, “waw; hook”), from Proto-Canaanite , from Proto-Sinaitic , from Egyptian 𓌉 representing a mace.
In Latin, ⟨V⟩ originally represented both the vowel /u/ and the consonant /w/; the distinct letterforms ⟨U⟩ and ⟨V⟩ became conventional from the 16th century.

1000017.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Latvian Latvija (“Latvia”). The Latvian name is a 19th-century formation from latvis (“Latvian, Lett”) and the country-name suffix -ija. It is first recorded in a Latvian text in 1862 and became established later in the century.
The underlying ethnonym is considerably older, but its deeper origin is uncertain. A connection with a local river name has been proposed.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Latvia, English Latvia, Finnish Latvia, Lithuanian Latvija, Serbo-Croatian Latvija and Slovene Latvija (“Latvia”).

1004369.etyen:
From djupe (“deep”) + vik (“bay, inlet”), literally “the deep bay”. The place-name type continues an Old Norse formation with djúpr (“deep”) and vík (“bay, inlet”). As a surname, it is habitational, originating from one of several farms or localities named Djupevik.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Djupevik, Swedish Djupvik and Danish Dybvig (“place name and surname”).

1004625.etyen:
From Eirik (“male given name”) + -s- (“genitive interfix”) + -son (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Eirik”. The given name Eirik is from Old Norse Eiríkr.
Compare Faroese Eiriksson and Icelandic Eiríksson (“patronymics meaning “son of Eirik””).

en.g: Brosundet; a strait in Ålesund, Møre og Romsdal, Norway, the inner-harbour waterway between Aspøya and Nørvøya

The old warehouses stand along Brosundet.
Fiskerinæringen la grunnlaget for plasseringen av byen, da Brosundet, eller den indre havn lå i le for vær og vind.
The fishing industry formed the basis for the location of the town, as Brosundet, or the inner harbour, was sheltered from the weather and wind.

1004881.etyen:
By surface analysis, bro (“bridge”) + sund (“sound, strait”), with the neuter definite singular ending -et; literally “the bridge sound”.
The precise historical motivation for the name is uncertain. The name is used for the inner-harbour stretch of the sound in central Ålesund, crossed by Hellebroa.
